tldr: By isolating the redundant tactile changes that vision and executed actions can already predict, and turning only the unexplained contact dynamics (tactile innovation) into a discrete code for auxiliary training, this method dramatically improves the contact-rich manipulation performance of visuo-tactile VLA models.
hero_caption: Model architecture of TacInno-VLA. Tactile tokens and code queries are inserted into the flow-matching Action Expert, which solves auxiliary tasks predicting tactile innovation codes and contact states only during training. At deployment, the tokenizer and auxiliary heads are completely detached for lightweight inference.
overview:
When robots perform delicate contact-rich tasks like insertion or slip control, tactile sensing should be essential. Recently, however, simply feeding tactile input into large Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has yielded inconsistent gains. Worse, models often rely so little on tactile input that their success rate barely drops when tactile input is disabled at test time. This happens because much of the tactile signal—such as gel deformation as the gripper closes—is already predictable from camera images and the robot's own executed actions. As both an input and a prediction target, this redundant information dominates training with trivial changes.

Inspired by estimation theory, the authors define the residual contact dynamics that cannot be explained by vision and executed actions as "tactile innovation." They use a VQ-VAE-based tokenizer to compress this innovation into a 16-bit discrete code, which the VLA's action generation backbone learns to predict from current observations via an auxiliary loss. Crucially, this code serves only as a training target, not an inference-time input. This sharpens the internal tactile representations toward truly essential contact dynamics without bloating the deployment architecture.

Evaluated across six simulation tasks and four real-world tasks on a Franka FR3, the model substantially outperformed existing visuo-tactile baselines. Furthermore, cutting off tactile input caused success rates to plummet, confirming that the policy genuinely relies on touch.
contributions: Uncovering the low tactile reliance of existing visuo-tactile policies through tactile-off tests, and tracing the root cause to redundant tactile information predictable from vision and executed actions.
Proposing a framework that conditions a tokenizer on vision and actions to isolate unexplained contact dynamics (tactile innovation) into a 16-bit discrete code.
Using the extracted code strictly as an auxiliary prediction target during training to shape internal tactile representations, adding zero computational overhead at deployment.

Demonstrating robust performance with average success rates of 87.5% across simulation and 70.5% across real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively.

sections.heading: Why hasn't adding touch sensors made robots smarter?
sections.summary: The paper highlights how many visuo-tactile VLA models barely rely on tactile inputs, identifying the culprit as redundant tactile changes predictable from vision and actions. It then introduces TacInno, which extracts only the unpredictable contact dynamics as an auxiliary training target.
sections.details:
Recently, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models fine-tuned from pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have drawn widespread interest in robotic manipulation. However, for contact-rich tasks like peg insertion or slip prevention, external cameras cannot fully capture subtle contact states. Consequently, researchers have turned to optical tactile sensors such as GelSight or DIGIT, which capture elastic gel deformation with internal cameras.

Yet existing visuo-tactile policies suffer from a serious issue: adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains or even hurts performance, and success rates barely change even when tactile input is disabled at test time (the tactile-off test). The authors trace this to the fundamental nature of tactile signals. Tactile sensing measures the contact surface response to the robot's own actions. Much of that signal—such as the gel indenting upon gripper closure—is readily predictable beforehand from visual observations and executed actions.

Directly feeding raw tactile data therefore injects redundant information that can cause overfitting. Meanwhile, using future tactile signals as prediction targets (like world models) causes losses to be dominated by trivial, predictable changes. To solve this, the authors coin the residual contact change that vision and action cannot explain as "tactile innovation," proposing TacInno to isolate it and use it as a supervisory training signal.

sections.heading: The evolution of tactile policies and discrete latent dynamics
sections.summary: The paper categorizes prior visuo-tactile policies into three development stages, outlines their limitations, and contextualizes how TacInno adapts discrete latent dynamics—traditionally used in video generation—for tactile innovation extraction.
sections.details:
### Trends in Visuo-Tactile Policy Learning
Prior approaches have evolved through three main stages. The first generation simply fed tactile images as additional inputs, relying solely on imitation learning's action loss. Because the action loss prioritizes overall trajectory matching, the model often ended up ignoring tactile signals. The second generation introduced tactile world models or auxiliary tasks predicting future tactile states, but wasted substantial capacity predicting stationary, non-contact phases. The third generation weighted prediction losses by tactile change magnitude. However, the largest changes are precisely the trivial ones most predictable from actions, leaving the underlying problem unsolved. TacInno fundamentally differs by supervising solely on what vision and actions cannot explain.

### Applying Discrete Latent Dynamics Learning
Discrete representation learning using VQ-VAEs has flourished in models like Genie and LAPA to extract unobserved latent actions from video transitions. TacInno adopts a similar formulation, but because it operates on demonstration data where the robot's actions are known, it introduces a key novelty: conditioning both the encoder and decoder on known visual observations and executed actions. This allows the decoder to bypass predictable dynamics, forcing the codebook to bottle only the residual, unexplained contact dynamics.

sections.heading: Encoding the unpredictable: how TacInno teaches contact to the action model
sections.summary: This section details the formulation of tactile innovation by subtracting vision- and action-predictable changes, the spatio-temporal Transformer tokenizer compressing it into a 16-bit code, and the TacInno-VLA policy trained with auxiliary code prediction.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Tactile Innovation
The policy takes visual observations $o_t$, language instruction $\ell$, proprioception $q_t$, and tactile observations $X_t$ (indentation depth maps and marker displacement fields) to predict an action chunk of future steps $a_{t+1:t+H}$. The cumulative tactile change $\Delta X$ from step $t$ to $t+5k$ ($k\in\{1,2,3\}$) is decomposed into an expected change predictable from current touch, future vision, and executed actions, plus an unexplained residual $\nu$ termed tactile innovation. Future vision is conditioned because contact changes visible in camera frames need not be redundantly encoded by tactile signals.

### 3.2 TacInno Tokenizer
Because the residual $\nu$ is a high-dimensional pixel field, it cannot serve directly as a policy prediction target. TacInno compresses it into a discrete code $c_t$ consisting of 4 tokens (16 entries each, 16 bits total). A spatio-temporal Transformer conditions both its encoder and decoder on image tokens (DINOv2 features) and action tokens. With direct access to vision and actions, the decoder creates strong incentives for the codebook to retain only what cannot be reconstructed from them—the tactile innovation. To capture temporally evolving events such as incipient slip, causal temporal attention encodes across four frames at $t, t+5, t+10, t+15$.

### 3.3 TacInno-VLA Policy
The action policy builds on $\pi_{0.5}$, consisting of a PaliGemma-based VLM backbone and a 300M-parameter flow-matching Action Expert. Sixty tactile tokens from three historical frames and four learnable code queries are fed into the Action Expert. A key architectural mechanism is block-wise attention masking: code queries can attend to tactile and visual tokens, but action tokens are strictly blocked from attending to code queries. This allows gradients from code prediction to flow into shared tactile representations without contaminating the inference-time action generation path. At deployment, the tokenizer and auxiliary heads are discarded, introducing zero extra computational burden.

captions.F2: Architecture of the TacInno tokenizer. Conditioning both encoder and decoder on visual features (DINOv2) and actions forces code $c_t$ to bottle only the tactile innovation unexplained by vision and action.

sections.heading: Does it really use touch? Rigorous testing in simulation and real-world setups
sections.summary: TacInno-VLA was evaluated on six UniVTAC simulation tasks and four real-world tasks. Ablations verified its core architectural choices, while tactile-off tests and information-theoretic probing confirmed that the model genuinely relies on tactile innovation.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
Six contact-rich tasks from the UniVTAC benchmark were selected: peg insertion, tube insertion, can lifting, bottle lifting, key pulling, and bottle shelving, using 50 demonstrations per task. On real hardware, a Franka FR3 arm with Xense tactile sensors was evaluated across four tasks (45 demonstrations each): blackboard erasing, socket plugging, uprighting a tipped can, and opening a bottle cap. Baselines included state-of-the-art visuo-tactile methods such as SimpleTouch, $\mathcal{N}_0$-VTLA, FTP-1, FTP-$\pi_{0.5}$, and UniVTAC-ACT.

### 4.2 Simulation Results and Ablations
In simulation, TacInno-VLA achieved an average success rate of 87.5%, outperforming the strongest baseline (SimpleTouch at 76.8%) by 10.7 percentage points, while maintaining over 75% success across every single task. In ablation studies, encoding all tactile changes without conditioning caused performance to plunge by 21.0 percentage points, and conditioning only on images dropped it by 13.5 points. Removing action conditioning resulted in codes overwhelmed by predictable gripper closure deformations.

### 4.3 Tactile Reliance and Probing Analysis
When tactile inputs were replaced with blank dummy frames at test time (tactile-off test), baseline success rates barely dropped, revealing their near-total neglect of touch. In contrast, TacInno-VLA's success rate in the can lifting task collapsed from 88% to 0%, proving critical reliance on tactile signals. Probing analysis also confirmed ideal behavior: the proportion explained by the code showed sharp peaks right at contact and incipient slip, dropping to zero once the can's tilt became visible to camera views.

### 4.4 Real-World Experiments
In real-world tasks, TacInno-VLA achieved an average success rate of 70.5%, significantly exceeding SimpleTouch (61.5%) and FTP-1 (58.5%). Removing the auxiliary code prediction loss dropped success to 47.5%—lower even than running without tactile input entirely (51.5%). This confirms that tactile innovation auxiliary supervision plays a decisive role in real hardware environments.

captions.F4: Temporal evolution of tactile innovation during a can lifting demonstration. As shown on the right, the code's explanatory proportion (orange) surges before contact (a) and at incipient slip (c), but vanishes once the can's tilt becomes visible to cameras (d onward).

sections.heading: Conclusions and broad implications
sections.summary: By targeting tactile innovation unexplained by vision and action as an auxiliary training objective, TacInno dramatically elevates VLA contact manipulation. This innovation concept holds promise beyond touch to other sensor modalities.
sections.details:
This work addressed the inherent redundancy in visuo-tactile VLA models, where much of the tactile feedback duplicates what is already evident from vision and executed actions. TacInno extracts and trains on this residual "tactile innovation." Using a conditional multi-frame tokenizer, it compresses residual contact dynamics into a 16-bit discrete code, honing the policy's internal tactile representations without adding any deployment overhead.

Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrated that TacInno overcomes the superficial tactile reliance of previous methods, unlocking genuinely touch-dependent dexterous manipulation. The authors conclude that supervising models strictly on the "innovation" unexplained by other modalities provides a general, promising paradigm applicable to other multimodal robotic settings, including audio and force-torque sensing.

takeaways: In multimodal learning, if a sensor input is largely predictable from other modalities or executed actions, using it raw as an input or target leads the model to be dominated by trivial signals.
Conditioning a reconstruction task on known signals allows an information bottleneck (like a VQ-VAE code) to concentrate solely on truly unpredictable, novel information (innovation).
Using extracted high-level codes purely as auxiliary prediction targets during training—rather than deployment inputs—shapes internal representations effectively with zero inference overhead.
When evaluating tactile models, simple success rates are not enough; conducting a tactile-off test (measuring performance drop when touch is disabled) is essential to verify genuine sensory reliance.
limitations: The tokenizer operates over a fixed temporal window (15 steps), which may struggle with very long-horizon contact dynamics or, conversely, extremely instantaneous impacts.
An extra pretraining pipeline is required to learn the tactile innovation tokenizer, adding a staged training step compared to pure end-to-end learning.

The architecture is designed around vision-based tactile sensors (GelSight/Xense) with indentation maps and marker displacement fields; applicability to 1-axis or 6-axis force-torque sensors remains unverified.
